newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: RTRS-Australia GDP shows inflation not a concern.
newsitem.headline: RTRS-Australia GDP shows inflation not a concern.

text.p: Economic growth data has confirmed Australia's status as a low inflation country, and left open the possibility of a further cut in interest rates early next year.

With the economy likely to remain slow in the December quarter, and with excess capacity existing in an economy performing patchily, analysts said the Reserve Bank of Australia (RBA) could cut interest rates without threatening inflation.
Gross domestic product (GDP) grew by 0.8 percent in the Setpember quarter, to be 3.8 percent higher over the year, official figures released on Wednesday showed.
The figures confirmed the slowing in the annual pace of growth, from over five percent earlier this year.
They also showed that while the economy was growing, activity across different sectors was patchy.

"I think this shows that the problem with the Australian economy is not that it's about to stall, it's that it's essentially still stuck in second gear," said Bankers Trust Australia chief economist Chris Caton.
Of most surprise to economists was a 0.4 percent fall in the GDP(E) deflator -- a broad based measure of inflationary pressures in the economy.
Over the year, the deflator rose by only 1.3 percent. Over the same period the consumer price index (CPI) rose 2.1 percent.
"That to me was surprisingly good news," Commonwealth Bank chief economist Bruce Freeland said. "It really is a good result, it's confimration of our low inflation status."
"I'm sure that the Reserve Bank is quite pleased to see that, because the GDP deflator is obviously a much broader measure of inflation than the CPI," he said.
The combination of slowing growth, benign inflation and some excess capictiy in the economy meant a rate cut as a means of boosting activity could be delivered, other analysts said.

"Inflation is not really a hurdle at this point for another rate cut - it depends whether the economy's got enough steam now to chug up to four percent and stay there or whether it needs another rate cut in order to maintain this sort of growth rate," Dresdner Australia chief economist Rob Henderson said.
However, any cut would be more likely early next year than this year, economists said.

The RBA Board meet on Tuesday, but no change was announced on Wednesday morning. The board next meets in early February, although it is possible for the RBA to change monetary possible on any day it chooses.
"I think the Bank is taking a softly, softly approach," Bankers Trust's Caton said.
"They're very keen to emphasise that they're easing because inflation is as good as it is."

"They'll wait for one more round of good inflation figures before they cut again. Given how soft the economy is, we will almost certainly get another rate decrease, but in early February, not today," he said.
Official interest rates currently stand at 6.5 percent, having been eased by 50 percentage points on both July 31 and November 6.

While the September GDP data was somewhat dated, and did not show the impact of the July rate cut, economists said that the partial indicators already released for the December quarter suggested growth would remain sluggish.
"The economy is still flat, domestic demand is broadly flat looking at the June and September figures together," Colonial State Bank senior economist Craig James said.
"With inflation very well restrained and high real interest rates, there is overwhelming justification for a further cut in interest rates," he said.
-- Sydney Newsroom 61-2 9373-1800
